summary: Gives guidance on implementing and using TCP in constrained-node networks, as found in Internet of Things settings. These need small implementations and often skip optional features, and the document explains techniques that simplify TCP while keeping it working.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny gadgets cannot run all of TCP's features. This explains which parts a small device can skip and still talk reliably.

questions: lightweight tcp implementation for constrained networks
how to implement tcp for iot devices
subtitle: How to use the Transmission Control Protocol on devices with limited resources.

tldr.problem: TCP is complex and requires significant memory and processing power. Internet of Things devices are often constrained and need to run TCP with minimal resources.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9006 provides guidance on implementing and configuring TCP in constrained-node networks. It explains which optional features to skip, how to tune parameters, and which techniques work best in different scenarios.
tldr.outcome: IoT devices can run lightweight, interoperable TCP implementations that maintain compatibility with standard TCP while using far less memory and consuming less energy.

today: RFC 9006 is an Informational RFC published in March 2021. It remains the primary guidance document for deploying TCP in IoT and constrained-node networks. The techniques it describes are in active use in production IoT deployments worldwide.

sections.title: TCP in the Internet of Things
sections.content:
The Internet of Things connects billions of small devices to the Internet. While most people think of UDP (a simpler protocol) when they think of IoT, TCP (the Transmission Control Protocol) is becoming more common. TCP ensures that data arrives in order and without loss, which some IoT applications need. However, TCP is complex and traditionally designed for powerful computers with plenty of memory.

This RFC provides guidance for embedded developers on implementing TCP on constrained devices: those with limited CPU power, small amounts of RAM, and batteries that must last a long time. The document is not a specification or a standard, but rather a collection of tried-and-tested techniques that let IoT devices run real TCP and stay compatible with standard TCP endpoints on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Most secure web connections use TCP. It checks that data arrives correctly, but the rules are complicated. For tiny smart devices, this RFC explains how to use TCP without using much memory or battery power.

sections.title: Challenges of Constrained Networks
sections.content:
Constrained-node networks have special characteristics that TCP was not originally designed for. Devices often have limited processing power and memory, sometimes as little as a few kilobytes of RAM. Radio links in IoT networks often drop packets (high loss rates), have low data rates (sometimes below 1 Mbps), and are asymmetric (one direction may be faster or less lossy than the other).

Energy is another constraint. Many IoT devices run on batteries and cannot afford to transmit unnecessary data or keep the radio powered on constantly. Some devices use radio duty-cycling: they turn the radio off for most of the time to save power, which means communication becomes bursty and unpredictable.

A typical IoT scenario has a small constrained device communicating with a large, powerful server on the Internet. The two endpoints may be separated by middleboxes like firewalls and NAT devices, which add complexity. Applications in this setting often involve uploading sensor readings (unidirectional), responding to commands (request-response), or downloading firmware updates (bulk transfer).
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny IoT devices have weak radios, little memory, and run on batteries. The networks they use drop more packets than the Internet, and devices sleep a lot to save power. TCP was designed for always-on computers, so IoT needs special tuning.

sections.title: Building Lightweight TCP Stacks
sections.content:
The simplest approach is a single-MSS stack. The Maximum Segment Size (MSS) is the biggest chunk of data TCP sends in one packet. A single-MSS stack only keeps one MSS of unacknowledged data in flight at a time, which simplifies the implementation dramatically. The receiver advertises a window of just 1 MSS, and both congestion control and flow control become trivial.

This approach works well for small messages (under about 1220 bytes in IPv6), but it suffers from poor performance for larger transfers because it becomes a stop-and-wait protocol: send one packet, wait for acknowledgment, send the next. Firmware updates or bulk sensor uploads become very slow.

To reduce code size, implementations can skip many optional TCP features. They must support only the MSS option, No-Operation, and End-of-Options. TCP options like Window Scale (for windows bigger than 64 kB), Timestamps (for detecting false timeouts), SACK (Selective Acknowledgments, for efficient retransmission), and TCP-Timestamps are not required for basic interoperability.

For devices with more resources, a larger window (3 to 5 MSS or more) allows using Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery, which are more efficient than waiting for timeouts. Such a device can also benefit from Selective Acknowledgments (SACK), which help identify exactly which packets the receiver is missing.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest approach sends one chunk of data, waits for a confirmation, then sends the next chunk. This is slow but easy and uses little memory. Bigger devices can send several chunks before waiting, which is faster.

sections.title: Tuning TCP for IoT
sections.content:
Several TCP parameters need careful tuning in constrained networks. The Maximum Segment Size (MSS) should be set to avoid IP fragmentation. An IPv6 datagram that exceeds 1280 bytes must be reassembled on the receiving end. Most IoT devices can handle an MSS of 1220 bytes (leaving room for IP and TCP headers) without triggering fragmentation. However, devices using technologies with larger frame sizes (like NB-IoT with 1600-byte MTU or IEEE 802.11ah with up to 7991 bytes) can safely use larger MSS values.

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) is valuable in IoT networks. Instead of dropping packets to signal congestion, a router can mark a packet's header, and the receiver echoes this back. The sender then reduces its sending rate without losing data. This saves energy by avoiding retransmissions, but it adds complexity to the implementation.

Delayed Acknowledgments reduce overhead by combining multiple ACKs into one. However, for unidirectional IoT traffic (like sensor uploads), Delayed ACKs can waste time and battery. In request-response patterns, enabling them on the server helps combine responses with ACKs. The trade-off depends on traffic patterns and must be tuned per deployment.

The Initial Window (how many packets a sender starts with) is often set to 10 MSS for broadband. But IoT device radios may buffer only 1 to 3 MSS worth of data, so a 10-MSS burst overflows the buffer. A smaller initial window prevents data loss.

The Retransmission Timeout (RTO) algorithm determines how long to wait before assuming a packet is lost and resending it. In constrained networks with variable delays, short timeouts risk spurious retransmissions (wasting energy), while long timeouts waste time. Adaptive RTO algorithms from CoAP over UDP have been shown to work well in IoT.
sections.plainLanguage: Several dials control TCP's behavior: how big each packet is, whether congestion is signaled without losing data, how long to wait for confirmations, and how long before assuming something is lost. Each dial has a trade-off between speed and energy.

sections.title: Connection Management in IoT
sections.content:
IoT applications should think carefully about how long to keep TCP connections open. A constrained device initiates connections to let it sleep between transmissions. However, keeping a connection open uses resources. If the connection is idle for too long, middleboxes (firewalls, NATs) may delete their state, breaking the connection. RFC 5382 specifies a minimum idle timeout of 124 minutes, but measurements show many NATs drop connections after 2 to 60 minutes.

Applications have three strategies. First, short-lived connections: close the connection after each exchange. This wastes resources on three-way handshakes but avoids idle timeouts. TCP Fast Open (TFO) reduces this overhead by allowing data in the initial SYN packet, but it adds complexity and security considerations. Second, long-lived connections with heartbeats: keep one connection open and send periodic application-level heartbeat messages to prevent middleboxes from timing out. This saves handshake overhead but consumes energy on heartbeats. Third, use TCP keep-alive probes (though these default to no less than 2 hours, making them impractical for most IoT).

Limiting concurrent connections is important. Each connection requires memory for a Transmission Control Block (TCB). Constrained devices should minimize the number of simultaneous connections. Using multiple connections for performance (like HTTP/1.1 pipelining) is generally discouraged in IoT to avoid middlebox issues and congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny devices have choices: close the connection quickly (uses energy on handshakes), keep it open with heartbeat messages (uses energy on pings), or rarely check if it is still alive. Each has costs.

sections.title: Security and Robustness
sections.content:
TCP itself provides no encryption. All applications should use TLS (Transport Layer Security) to protect the contents of TCP messages. TLS adds overhead, but it is strongly recommended even in constrained environments. For transport-layer security, TCP-AO (TCP Authentication Option) can sign packets, but it adds 16 to 20 bytes per packet and increases complexity.

Constrained devices are vulnerable to DoS (Denial of Service) attacks. The shrew attack exploits timeouts by sending packets timed to coincide with RTO expiration. Devices with small windows that rely on timeouts for loss recovery are particularly vulnerable. Defenses include randomizing RTO values and having routers detect and block shrew-like traffic patterns.

Because constrained devices have limited processing power, they may appear to attackers as attractive targets for botnet recruitment or as victims of bandwidth exhaustion attacks. Deploying constrained devices should include consideration of network-level DDoS protection.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP data is not secret. Use TLS (HTTPS) to scramble it. Tiny devices are tempting targets for hackers, so hide data and use randomness to avoid predictable timeouts that attackers can exploit.
